'''Alexander Craig Aitken''' {{postnominals|country=GBR|FRS|FRSE|FRSL}} {{postnominals|country=NZL|FRSNZ}} (1 April 1895–3 November 1967) was one of [[New Zealand]]'s most eminent mathematicians.<ref name="edge">{{cite web|url=http://www.nzedge.com/heroes/aitken.html|title=Alexander Aitken THE HUMAN COMPUTER|publisher=NZ Edge|access-date=7 December 2005|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20090203193156/http://nzedge.com/heroes/aitken.html|archive-date=3 February 2009|url-status=dead}}</ref><ref name="actuator">{{MacTutor|id=Aitken|title=Alexander Aitken}}</ref> In a 1935 paper he introduced the concept of [[generalized least squares]], along with now standard [[Matrix (mathematics)|vector/matrix notation]] for the [[linear regression model]].<ref>{{cite journal | last1 = Aitken | first1 = A. C. | year = 1935 | title = On Least Squares and Linear Combinations of Observations | journal = Proceedings of the Royal Society of Edinburgh | volume = 55 | pages = 42–48 | doi = 10.1017/s0370164600014346 }}</ref> Another influential paper co-authored with his student [[Harold Silverstone]] established the lower bound on the variance of an [[estimator]],<ref>{{cite journal | last1 = Aitken | first1 = A. C. | last2 = Silverstone | first2 = H. | year = 1942 | title = On the Estimation of Statistical Parameters | journal = Proceedings of the Royal Society of Edinburgh | volume = 61 | issue = 2| pages = 186–194 | doi = 10.1017/s008045410000618x | s2cid = 124029876 }}</ref> now known as [[Cramér–Rao bound]].<ref>{{cite journal |first=L. R. |last=Shenton |title=The so-called Cramer–Rao inequality |journal=[[The American Statistician]] |year=1970 |volume=24 |issue=2 |page=36 |jstor=2681931 }}</ref> He was elected to the [[Royal Society of Literature]] for his [[World War I]] memoir, ''Gallipoli to the Somme''.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.stuff.co.nz/entertainment/103175807/review-gallipoli-to-the-somme-recollections-of-a-new-zealand-infantryman-by-alexander-aitken|title=Review: Gallipoli to the Somme: Recollections of a New Zealand Infantryman by Alexander Aitken|website=Stuff|date=21 April 2018|language=en|access-date=2019-05-01}}</ref>

==Life and work==
Aitken was born on 1 April 1895 in [[Dunedin]], the eldest of the seven children of  Elizabeth Towers and William Aitken. He was of Scottish descent, his grandfather having emigrated from [[Lanarkshire]] in 1868. His mother was from [[Wolverhampton]].<ref name="royalsocietypublishing.org">{{Cite journal|doi = 10.1098/rsbm.1968.0001|title = Alexander Craig Aitken, 1895-1967|year = 1968|last1 = Whittaker|first1 = John Macnaghten|last2 = Bartlett|first2 = Maurice Stevenson|journal = Biographical Memoirs of Fellows of the Royal Society|volume = 14|pages = 1–14|s2cid = 121731388|doi-access = free}}</ref>

He was educated at [[Otago Boys' High School]] in Dunedin (1908–13) where he was school [[dux]] and won the Thomas Baker Calculus Scholarship in his last year at school. He saw active service during [[World War I]] enlisting in April 1915 with the [[New Zealand Expeditionary Force]], and serving in [[Gallipoli Campaign|Gallipoli]] from November 1915, in Egypt, and at the [[Western Front (World War I)|Western Front]]. He was seriously wounded at the [[Battle of the Somme|Somme]].<ref>A. C. Aitken (1963). ''Gallipoli to the Somme: Recollections of a New Zealand infantryman''. Oxford.</ref> He spent several months in hospital in [[Chelsea, London|Chelsea]] before being invalided out of the army and shipped home to New Zealand in March 1917.<ref name="royalsocietypublishing.org"/>

Resuming his studies Aitken graduated with an [[Master of Arts|MA]] degree from the [[University of Otago]] in 1920, then worked as a schoolmaster at Otago Boys' High School from 1920 to 1923.

Aitken studied for a doctorate ([[Doctor of Philosophy|PhD]]) at the [[University of Edinburgh]], in Scotland, under [[Edmund Taylor Whittaker]] where his dissertation, "The Graduation of Observational Data", was considered so impressive that he was awarded a [[Doctor of Science|DSc]] degree in 1925.<ref>{{Cite thesis |last=Aitken|first=A. C.|date=1925|title=The Graduation of Observational Data |publisher=University of Edinburgh |type=DSc |language=en|hdl=1842/26479}}</ref><ref name="edge" /> Aitken's impact at the university had been so great that he had been elected a [[Fellow of the Royal Society of Edinburgh]] (FRSE) the year before the award of his degree, upon the proposal of [[Sir Edmund Whittaker]], [[Sir Charles Galton Darwin]], [[Edward Copson]] and [[David Gibb (mathematician)|David Gibb]]. In 1927, Aitken published what became known as [[Aitken delta-squared process]] as part of an extension to [[Bernoulli's method]].<ref name="aitken">{{cite journal |last1=Aitken |first1=A. C. |title=XXV.—On Bernoulli's Numerical Solution of Algebraic Equations |journal=Proceedings of the Royal Society of Edinburgh |date=January 1927 |volume=46 |pages=289–305 |doi=10.1017/S0370164600022070}}</ref><ref name="genesis-aitken">{{cite journal |last1=Brezinski |first1=Claude |last2=Redivo–Zaglia |first2=Michela |title=The genesis and early developments of Aitken's process, Shanks' transformation, the ε–algorithm, and related fixed point methods |journal=Numerical Algorithms |date=January 2019 |volume=80 |issue=1 |pages=11–133 |doi=10.1007/s11075-018-0567-2}}</ref>  Aitken was awarded the Makdougall-Brisbane Prize for 1930–32, and was active in the affairs of the RSE, serving as Councillor (1934–36), Secretary to Ordinary Meetings (1936–40), and vice-president (1948–51; 1956–59). He was also an active member of the [[Edinburgh Mathematical Society]] and a Fellow of the [[Faculty of Actuaries]].

Aitken spent his entire career at the University of Edinburgh, working as lecturer in Actuarial Mathematics & Statistics (1925–36), Reader in Statistics (1936–46), and finally Professor of Mathematics (1946–65).

During [[World War II]] he worked in [[Hut 6]] [[Bletchley Park]] decrypting [[ENIGMA]] code.<ref name="odbn">{{Cite ODNB| title = Aitken, Alexander Craig | doi = 10.1093/ref:odnb/30357 | year = 2004 | pmid =  | pmc = }}</ref>

Aitken was one of the best [[mental calculator]]s known, and had a prodigious memory. This ability was researched by the psychologist [[Ian M.L. Hunter]]. He knew the first 1000 digits of <math>\pi</math>, the 96 recurring digits of 1/97, and memorised the ''[[Aeneid]]'' in high school. However, his inability to forget the horrors he witnessed in [[World War I]] led to recurrent [[Major depressive disorder|depression]] throughout his life.<ref name="edge" />

Aitken was elected a [[Fellow of the Royal Society]] (FRS) in 1936<ref name="frs"/> and an [[Fellow of the Royal Society of New Zealand|Honorary Fellow of the Royal Society of New Zealand]] (Hon FRSNZ) in 1940,<ref>[http://www.royalsociety.org.nz/publications/reports/yearbooks/year2000/past-honorary-fellows/ Honorary Fellows, 1870-2000] - website of the Royal Society of New Zealand</ref> both for his work in statistics, [[algebra]] and [[numerical analysis]]. He was an accomplished writer, being elected a [[Fellow of the Royal Society of Literature]] (FRSL) in 1964 in response to the publication of his war memoirs, ''Gallipoli to the Somme''.<ref>{{Cite book|last=Aitken|first=A. C|title=Gallipoli to the Somme. Recollections of a New Zealand infantryman, etc. [With a map.|date=1963|location=London|language=English|oclc=1221768576}}</ref> His book was the basis of an [[oratorio]] of the same name by the New Zealand composer [[Anthony Ritchie]].<ref>{{Cite book|last=Ritchie|first=Anthony|url=https://natlib-primo.hosted.exlibrisgroup.com/NLNZ:NLNZ:NLNZ_ALMA21296334190002836|title=Gallipoli to the Somme: for soprano, bass, choir and orchestra|date=2016|oclc=1142393027}}</ref> He was also an excellent musician, being described by [[Eric Fenby]] as the most accomplished amateur musician he had ever known, and was a champion athlete in his younger days.

==Awards and honours==

The [[New Zealand Mathematical Society]] and [[London Mathematical Society]] [[Aitken Lectureship]] occurs every two years (in odd-numbered years) when a mathematician from New Zealand is invited by both Societies to give lectures at different universities around the UK over a period of several weeks.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://nzmathsoc.org.nz/?activities |website=New Zealand Mathematical Society |accessdate=20 July 2018|title=Activities of the Society }}</ref><ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.lms.ac.uk/events/lectures/forder-and-aitken-lectureship |website=London Mathematical Society |title=LMS-NZMS Forder and Aitken Lectureships|accessdate=20 July 2018}}</ref>

An annual "Aitken Prize" is awarded by the [[New Zealand Mathematical Society]] for the best student talk at their colloquium. The prize was inaugurated in 1995 at the [[University of Otago]]'s Aitken Centenary Conference, a joint mathematics and statistics conference held to remember Aitken 100 years after his birth.

==Personal life==
He married [[Winifred Betts]], a lecturer in biology and the first female lecturer appointed to the University of Otago, in 1920. They had a daughter and a son. Aitken died on 3 November 1967, in [[Edinburgh]].
